Spatial cross-validation

Justin Chase

Source: vignettes/spatial-cross-validation.Rmd
spatial-cross-validation.Rmd

This article shows what a cross-validated error measures, how to choose folds whose score matches the map you will make, how to size the blocks, and how to read every part of the result.

This article needs two optional packages: gstat for the autocorrelation range and ggplot2 for the figures. Where one is missing, the code that needs it is shown but not run.

What a cross-validated error measures

A random fold puts a held-out point’s neighbours in the training set. When the field is spatially autocorrelated, those neighbours carry the held-out point’s value, and a model that draws on nearby observations uses them. The cross-validation score then measures the error of predicting among the samples. Blocks hold out whole areas, and their score measures the error of predicting into an unsampled gap the size of a block (Roberts et al. 2017).

A cross-validated error is the error at the distance the folds put between the held-out points and their training data. It reads low for a map whose locations sit farther from the data than that, and high for one whose locations sit closer.

A learner and a simulated field

Each function that scores a model takes the folds from make_folds() through its folds argument: cv_rf(), cv_gwr() and cv_bayes() for the built-in backends, compare_models_cv() to score several on the same folds, and cv_spatial() for a learner of your own. This article uses a five-nearest-neighbour smoother written for cv_spatial(). It needs no optional package and predicts from the five nearest observations alone, so how far the folds hold those observations away decides its score.

library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

knn_fit <- function(train_sf, response_var = "z", k = 5L) {
  new_spatial_fit(
    subclass       = "knnsurf_fit",
    engine         = list(xy = st_coordinates(train_sf),
                          y = st_drop_geometry(train_sf)[[response_var]],
                          k = k),
    formula        = as.formula(paste(response_var, "~ 1")),
    response_var   = response_var,
    predictor_vars = character(0),
    data_sf        = train_sf
  )
}

predict.knnsurf_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
  e  <- object$engine
  xy <- if (is.null(newdata)) e$xy else st_coordinates(newdata)
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(xy)), function(i) {
    d <- sqrt((e$xy[, 1] - xy[i, 1])^2 + (e$xy[, 2] - xy[i, 2])^2)
    mean(e$y[order(d)[seq_len(min(e$k, length(d)))]])
  }, numeric(1))
}
registerS3method("predict", "knnsurf_fit", predict.knnsurf_fit)

knn_fn <- function(train_sf, ...) knn_fit(train_sf, "z", k = 5L)

cv_spatial() needs only the constructor and a predict() method. ?new_spatial_fit lists what summary() and model_metrics() need on top of that, and vignette("models") explains the pattern.

The data are 400 points in a 1,000 m square (EPSG:32632) over a simulated exponential field with range parameter 60 m, so its correlation falls to 5 percent at about 180 m, three times the range parameter. The sd = 0.3 term adds measurement noise.

set.seed(7)
n  <- 400
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 60) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
        rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
pts  <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)

Random folds against blocks

The next chunk scores the same learner on the same data with random folds and with blocks, and prints the size of the blocks built.

fr <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fb <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 200, seed = 1)
c(width = fb$params$block_width, height = fb$params$block_height)
##    width   height 
## 247.0732 249.3515
cv_random  <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = fr)
cv_blocked <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = fb)

c(random  = cv_random$overall$RMSE,
  blocked = cv_blocked$overall$RMSE,
  ratio   = cv_blocked$overall$RMSE / cv_random$overall$RMSE)
##    random   blocked     ratio 
## 0.7839092 1.0086341 1.2866722

block_size is the smallest edge a block may have. make_folds() fits a whole number of blocks across each axis, so over this square block_size = 200 builds a 4 by 4 grid of blocks 247 m wide and 249 m tall, wider than the 180 m range. “Choosing a block size” below sizes the blocks from the data. Without folds, cv_spatial() builds block folds itself; build them with make_folds() when you want to inspect or reuse them.

Blocked folds put the error 29 percent higher on this fixture. Both numbers come from the same 400 observations and the same smoother; only the fold assignment differs.

Two choices made outside the folds change what either score measures. A model given the coordinates as predictors (fit_rf_model(include_coords = TRUE)) can learn the training surface by location, so its error grows quickly with the distance from the data. Predictors chosen on the whole data set have seen every held-out row, and select_features_forward() chooses them inside the folds instead. vignette("models") covers both.

Which score matches your map

The number that applies depends on where the map predicts. fold_separation() takes the locations the map will predict at and compares two sets of distances: from each of those locations to the nearest training point, and from each held-out point to the nearest point of its fold’s training data. Here the map is a 30 by 30 grid of points over the square, and reading() returns the one-word reading of a set of folds against it.

map_pts <- st_make_grid(pts, n = c(30, 30), what = "centers")

reading <- function(folds, data = pts) {
  sep <- fold_separation(folds, data, prediction_points = map_pts)
  attr(sep, "target")$reading
}
c(random = reading(fr), blocked = reading(fb))
##    random   blocked 
## "matched" "farther"

The reading is one of four:

  • "matched": the held-out points sit about as far from their training data as the map’s points do, so the score estimates the error at the map’s distances.
  • "farther": they sit farther, and the score tends to read high for this map.
  • "closer": they sit closer, and the score tends to read low for this map. Random folds on clustered samples, with a map of the whole region, read this way.
  • "mixed": closer at some distances and farther at others, so the distances give no single direction.

The reading compares nearest-neighbour distances only. On clustered samples, a learner that averages several neighbours can still score low when those distances match.

print() gives the distances fold by fold:

sep_blocked <- fold_separation(fb, pts, prediction_points = map_pts)
sep_blocked
## Fold separation: block_kfold, 5 fold(s), 400 held-out point(s) (EPSG:32632)
##   prediction target: 900 point(s), measured to each fold's training data
## 
##  fold n_train n_test n_blocks min_dist median_dist target   gap
##     1     322     78        3    27.33       90.32  27.35 61.75
##     2     324     76        3    12.77       76.32  27.44 43.02
##     3     307     93        4    12.77       83.85  28.87 46.78
##     4     323     77        3    14.66      127.40  27.33 91.32
##     5     324     76        3    14.66       86.82  27.52 51.98
## 
##   Held-out points sit a median of 89.72 from their nearest training
##   point; the closest is 12.77 away.
##   The prediction points sit a median of 27.56 from the same training data
##   (23.19 from the nearest of all sites). Held-out minus prediction:
##   +58.55 in mean distance (W1 58.55). The held-out points sit farther
##   from their training data than the prediction points do, so the
##   cross-validated error tends to read high for these prediction points.

min_dist and median_dist run from each held-out point to its nearest training point, target is the median distance from the map’s points to the same training data, and gap is the fold’s mean held-out distance minus its mean prediction distance. The lines under the table pool the folds: the held-out points sit a median of 89.7 m from their training data, and the map’s points 27.6 m.

Clustered samples

The points of this fixture cover the square evenly, so random folds read "matched" for a map of it. The next chunk keeps only the points within 120 m of six of them, a clustered sample, and reads random folds and kNNDM folds against the same map of the whole square.

set.seed(2)
centres <- pts[sample(nrow(pts), 6), ]
cl <- pts[lengths(st_is_within_distance(pts, centres, dist = 120)) > 0, ]
nrow(cl)
## [1] 102
fr_cl <- make_folds(cl, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fk_cl <- make_folds(cl, k = 5, method = "knndm", prediction_points = map_pts,
                    seed = 1)
c(random = reading(fr_cl, cl), knndm = reading(fk_cl, cl))
##    random     knndm 
##  "closer" "matched"
cv_random_cl <- cv_spatial(cl, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                           folds = fr_cl)
cv_knndm_cl  <- cv_spatial(cl, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                           folds = fk_cl)
c(random = cv_random_cl$overall$RMSE, knndm = cv_knndm_cl$overall$RMSE)
##    random     knndm 
## 0.7815208 1.2562404

Random folds read "closer": each held-out point keeps training points from its own cluster, a median of 27.8 m away, while the map’s points sit a median of 107 m from the same training data. method = "knndm" (Linnenbrink et al. 2024) builds k folds whose held-out distances come as close as it can to the distances from map_pts to the samples, here by grouping the samples into 8 clusters, and reads "matched". Its RMSE of 1.26, against 0.78 for random folds, is the score at the distances the map has to reach. For this five-neighbour learner it can still read low for this map, as the caveat on clustered samples above says.

The six fold schemes

make_folds(method = ) builds six fold schemes:

method held out in each fold also left out of training needs suits a map that
random_kfold a random 1/k of the rows nothing k predicts among the samples, over an area they cover evenly
block_kfold the points in whole blocks of a grid, or of blocks nothing k; optionally block_size, auto_range, block_nx/block_ny or blocks (otherwise about block_multiplier * k blocks) predicts into unsampled gaps about as wide as the blocks
buffered_loo one point every point within buffer of it buffer; max_test limits the number of fits predicts at a known distance from the data
leave_location_out every row of one or more locations nothing group_var predicts at sites with no measurements, from repeated measurements at others
nndm one point neighbours, chosen to match the prediction distances (Milà et al. 2022) prediction_points; at most 5,000 rows predicts at known locations, with a model cheap enough to refit once per point
knndm one of k folds, from clusters of the points or a random partition, whichever comes closer to the prediction distances nothing prediction_points predicts at known locations, from a larger layer or with a costly model

plot_folds() draws the assignment, with the blocks behind it when the scheme has any:

plot_folds(fb, pts)

Check whether any fold is a thin sliver or a single corner. If one is, change the block design: a different block_size, or polygons of your own through make_folds(blocks = ).

The next chunk runs three more schemes on the same data: kNNDM matched to the map’s points; buffered leave-one-out with a buffer of 180 m, the field’s effective range, scored on 50 of the points through max_test; and blocks taken from Voronoi cells around 16 k-means seeds in place of the grid. leave_location_out needs repeated measurements at the same sites, which this fixture does not have.

fk   <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "knndm", prediction_points = map_pts,
                   seed = 1)
floo <- make_folds(pts, method = "buffered_loo", buffer = 180, max_test = 50,
                   seed = 1)
vor  <- build_tessellation(voronoi_seeds_kmeans(pts, 16), quiet = TRUE)
fv   <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", blocks = vor$cells,
                   seed = 1)

schemes <- list(knndm = fk, buffered_loo = floo, voronoi_blocks = fv)
data.frame(
  folds   = sapply(schemes, function(f) f$k),
  reading = sapply(schemes, reading),
  RMSE    = sapply(schemes, function(f)
    cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = f)$overall$RMSE)
)
##                folds reading      RMSE
## knndm              5 matched 0.7839092
## buffered_loo      50 farther 1.1377276
## voronoi_blocks     5 farther 0.9957734

kNNDM keeps the random partition here (fk$params$chosen is "random"), as it does for samples spread evenly over the map. The 180 m buffer and the Voronoi blocks, about 254 m across, both hold the held-out points farther from their training data than the map’s points sit. make_folds(blocks = ) takes any polygons of your own the same way, such as the cells of another tessellation or a set of watersheds.

Choosing a block size

Make the blocks as wide as the gaps the map has to bridge. The wider the blocks, the farther the held-out points sit from their training data, and the score is the error at that distance.

From the autocorrelation range

The autocorrelation range is the distance beyond which two observations are close to uncorrelated. Using it as the smallest block edge is one way to choose the separation, and suits a map that has to reach that far from the data (Roberts et al. 2017; Valavi et al. 2019).

sac <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z")
c(range  = as.numeric(sac),
  nugget = sac_nugget(sac),
  sill   = sum(attr(sac, "variogram_model")$psill))
##       range      nugget        sill 
## 190.8824784   0.1404058   0.9942011

The estimated range, 190.9 m, is close to the 180 m the field was simulated with. sac_nugget() reads the nugget off the same fitted model; here it is 14 percent of the sill. A nugget that is most of the sill means nearby observations carry little information, and the blocked and random scores tend to be close.

plot() draws the variogram behind the estimate:

plot(sac)

The points are the empirical semivariances, sized by the number of point pairs behind each, the curve is the fitted model, and the dotted line marks the effective range given in the subtitle. When no range is identified, the subtitle gives the reason and no line is drawn.

make_folds(auto_range = TRUE) runs this estimate and uses it as the smallest block edge:

fa <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", response_var = "z",
                 auto_range = TRUE, seed = 1)
c(range  = as.numeric(fa$params$sac_range),
  width  = fa$params$block_width,
  height = fa$params$block_height)
##    range    width   height 
## 190.8825 197.6586 199.4812

The blocks are a little wider than the range because a whole number of them has to fit across the square.

When the variogram identifies no range, estimate_sac_range() returns NA with the reason attached. auto_range then warns and falls back to the default grid, about block_multiplier * k blocks over the extent (15 at k = 5), and you are back to choosing a size yourself. ?estimate_sac_range lists each reason and what it means, and plot() draws the variogram wherever one was computed.

The error at each block size

cv_block_size_sweep() runs the cross-validation at several block sizes and reports the curve, with a random-fold run as the reference. Each size is a full cross-validation, so five sizes at k = 5 make 25 fits, plus 5 for the random reference; max_fits caps that.

sw <- cv_block_size_sweep(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                          k = 5, n_sizes = 5, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
sw
## Cross-validation RMSE against block size (30 fits, k = 5, sizes in EPSG:32632)
##   estimated autocorrelation range: 190.9
##  block_size blocks_used k folds_ok  value fold_min fold_max
##      random          NA 5        5 0.7839   0.7534   0.8376
##       39.53         291 5        5 0.8139   0.6790   0.9040
##       67.32         169 5        5 0.8971   0.8740   0.9074
##      114.60          64 5        5 0.9734   0.7316   1.1559
##      195.20          25 5        5 1.0564   0.8429   1.2352
##      332.50           6 5        5 1.0968   1.0011   1.1759
plot(sw)

The error climbs away from the random-fold reference as the blocks widen, and the dotted line marks the estimated range. Each point of the curve is the error of a map whose locations sit as far from the data as that size’s held-out points do. To choose a size, run fold_separation() on the folds of each size, the $folds of each element of attr(sw, "results"), against the map’s points. block_size is the smallest edge asked for and block_width the edge built:

sizes <- data.frame(sw)[, c("block_size", "block_width", "value")]
sizes$reading <- sapply(attr(sw, "results"), function(r) reading(r$folds))
sizes
##   block_size block_width     value reading
## 1         NA          NA 0.7839092 matched
## 2   39.53171    39.53171 0.8138507 matched
## 3   67.32043    70.59234 0.8970955 farther
## 4  114.64316   123.53660 0.9733795 farther
## 5  195.23129   197.65855 1.0564147 farther
## 6  332.46864   494.14639 1.0968178 farther

For a map of this square the random folds read "matched", and so do the blocks asked for at 39.5 m. Their scores, 0.78 and 0.81, are the errors at the map’s distances; the larger sizes read "farther".

Watch blocks_used as the blocks grow. At the largest size, 332.5 m asked for and 494.1 m built, 6 blocks hold the points for 5 folds, so each fold holds out a large piece of the square. That score is the error of a map that has to reach across such a piece.

Reading a cross-validation result

overall is the pooled score and fold_metrics has one row per fold.

Spread across folds

plot_cv_metrics() shows the spread across folds. The pooled RMSE cannot tell one bad fold from an even spread of error; here the five blocked folds run from 0.94 to 1.12.

plot_cv_metrics(cv_blocked, metric = "RMSE")

Folds and rows accounted for

Two counts and four fields say what happened on the way through: n_folds_attempted against n_folds_succeeded; fold_status, one row per fold; n_dropped, rows removed for a missing or non-finite value; orphan_rows, rows no fold names; and n_unknown_ids, row IDs the folds name that the data do not have. On the clean run above nothing went missing:

c(attempted = cv_blocked$n_folds_attempted,
  succeeded = cv_blocked$n_folds_succeeded,
  dropped   = cv_blocked$n_dropped,
  orphans   = length(cv_blocked$orphan_rows),
  unknown   = cv_blocked$n_unknown_ids)
## attempted succeeded   dropped   orphans   unknown 
##         5         5         0         0         0

The next three runs each lose something: a learner that fails on one fold, data with three missing values scored on folds built on the first 300 rows, and the first 300 rows scored on folds built on all 400.

Folds that failed

The next chunk scores a learner that fails on one fold.

flaky <- function(train_sf, ...) {
  if (nrow(train_sf) < 320) stop("not enough training rows for this learner")
  knn_fit(train_sf, "z", k = 5L)
}
cv_flaky <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", character(0), fit_fn = flaky, folds = fb)
## Warning: cv_spatial(): 1 of 5 fold(s) failed (fold 3: error), so `overall`
## pools the other folds only and covers 307 of the 400 rows. A fold that fails is
## often the hardest to predict (a region or a factor level no training fold
## covers), so `overall` may flatter the model; `fold_status` gives each fold's
## cause.
cv_flaky$fold_status
##   fold status                                   message
## 1    1     ok                                          
## 2    2     ok                                          
## 3    3  error not enough training rows for this learner
## 4    4     ok                                          
## 5    5     ok
c(attempted = cv_flaky$n_folds_attempted,
  succeeded = cv_flaky$n_folds_succeeded)
## attempted succeeded 
##         5         4

fold_status names every fold supplied and what became of it, with the error text for the ones that failed. status is one of ok, error, skipped, dropped or worker_error. overall then pools the 4 folds that ran, 307 of the 400 rows, and cv_spatial() warns about it, since a fold that fails is often the hardest one to predict. fold_status keeps each cause with the result, so a script or a knitted report still has it after the console output is gone.

Rows left out 

holed <- pts
holed$z[c(3, 17, 42)] <- NA                       # three rows will be dropped
part  <- make_folds(pts[1:300, ], k = 4, method = "block_kfold", seed = 1)

cv_acc <- cv_spatial(holed, "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn, folds = part)
## Warning: prep_model_data(): dropped 3 of 400 row(s) (0.8%): 3 with a missing
## value, 0 with a non-finite value and 0 without a location (an empty point, or a
## coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150). Rows affected by column: z
## 3. The fit uses the 397 row(s) that remain; attr(, "dropped") lists the rows
## removed.
## Warning: cross-validation: 100 of 397 rows in the data are named by no fold
## (e.g. row ID 301, 302, 303). They enter no training set and are never scored.
## If the folds were built on a different or subsetted layer, rebuild them with
## make_folds() on this one.
c(n_dropped     = cv_acc$n_dropped,
  n_orphans     = length(cv_acc$orphan_rows),
  n_unknown_ids = cv_acc$n_unknown_ids)
##     n_dropped     n_orphans n_unknown_ids 
##             3           100             3

n_dropped is how many rows prep_model_data() removed for a missing or non-finite value before any fold was fitted. orphan_rows holds the row IDs no fold names, which here is rows 301 to 400, because the folds were built on the first 300. n_unknown_ids counts the distinct row IDs the folds name that the data do not have, which here is the three rows the NAs removed.

The two mirror each other, and which one is non-zero tells you which way the mismatch runs:

cv_rev <- cv_spatial(pts[1:300, ], "z", character(0), fit_fn = knn_fn,
                     folds = fb)
c(n_orphans = length(cv_rev$orphan_rows), n_unknown_ids = cv_rev$n_unknown_ids)
##     n_orphans n_unknown_ids 
##             0           100

Folds built on more rows than the data has give n_unknown_ids; folds built on fewer give orphan_rows. Rows in orphan_rows are never scored, so the score covers every observation only when orphan_rows is empty, no row was dropped and every fold ran. Unknown IDs cost the folds rows but leave every observation scored: the run above predicts 300 of its 300 rows.

Interval calibration (Bayesian GP)

A Bayesian GP predicts an interval for each held-out value, and a calibration check compares the share of values each interval contains with the share it claims. plot_calibration() draws, for each nominal level, the share of held-out values the intervals contained, pooled and fold by fold, from a cv_bayes() result. The chunk below is not run here, because it needs brms and a Stan toolchain and takes minutes. Nine coverage levels give a curve in place of the default three.

cvb <- cv_bayes(pts, "z", character(0), folds = fb,
                coverage_levels = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1),
                fit_args = list(chains = 2, iter = 1000))
plot_calibration(cvb)

Points below the diagonal are intervals that are too narrow: an 80 percent interval that contains 60 percent of the held-out values claims more certainty than the model has.

Next

The next article in reading order is vignette("models"), which fits the backends, compares them on the same folds, checks the residuals and maps where the predictions apply. vignette("reporting") lists what to report from a cross-validation. This article relied on ?make_folds, ?fold_separation, ?plot_folds, ?estimate_sac_range, ?sac_nugget, ?cv_block_size_sweep, ?cv_spatial, ?new_spatial_fit, ?plot_cv_metrics and ?plot_calibration. vignette("glossary") defines the terms it uses.

References

Linnenbrink, J., Milà, C., Ludwig, M. and Meyer, H. (2024). kNNDM CV: k-fold nearest-neighbour distance matching cross-validation for map accuracy estimation. Geoscientific Model Development 17, 5897–5912. https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-17-5897-2024

Milà, C., Mateu, J., Pebesma, E. and Meyer, H. (2022). Nearest neighbour distance matching leave-one-out cross-validation for map validation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 13(6), 1304–1316. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13851

Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40, 913–929. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881

Valavi, R., Elith, J., Lahoz-Monfort, J. J. and Guillera-Arroita, G. (2019). blockCV: An R package for generating spatially or environmentally separated folds for k-fold cross-validation of species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10, 225–232. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13107
